constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy
try hard not think about the trauma

Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

I have lost my connection to my community and culture

issues.explanation: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events are not well linked to the stated trauma of witnessing childhood domestic violence, especially when the other trigger items center on male presence and shouting. This trigger is not impossible, but in this profile it stands out as insufficiently connected to the rest of the formulation.

Listening for signs that someone is entering the home suggests a burglary/home-intrusion threat theme, which is weakly connected to the selected trauma-specific cues and memory/appraisal content centered on domestic violence. It pulls the threat profile toward external break-in danger rather than reenacted interpersonal violence.

Noticing weapons or dangerous objects in any environment implies a generalized weapon-attack threat theme, but the trauma type and the rest of the items do not support a weapon-focused formulation. This makes the threat node less coherent with the memory and appraisal content.

'I have failed in my most important role in life' is a broad role-failure appraisal that is not clearly anchored to the selected trauma memories or other appraisals. The other negative appraisals emphasize weakness and disconnection; this item introduces a different theme without enough support elsewhere in the profile.

Drug use is not well supported by the rest of the five-component profile. The strongest formulation link is Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies, and the other strategies clearly fit trigger-driven internal threat management, whereas drug use introduces a more severe coping pattern without corresponding support from the other selected items.

vignette: Mateo grew up in a tight-knit neighborhood where Sunday dinners were a sacred ritual, but inside his childhood home, the air would suddenly turn sharp. He remembers the exact moments like frozen frames: his father’s face contorted, the heavy thud of a fist against a doorframe, the sharp crack of ceramic shattering across the tiles. Those snapshots remain vivid and detailed, sitting in his mind like undeveloped photographs waiting to emerge. When he recalls those evenings now, a heavy guilt settles in his chest, as if his young presence was a failure to intervene. He tells himself he should have stopped it, that his silence made him complicit, and that conviction anchors a quiet shame he carries to this day. The habits born in that house followed him into his trade. For thirty years, Mateo has worked as a jeweler, his hands steady over magnifying loupes and fine chains, yet his eyes never stop scanning. When a male client steps into the shop, alone and asking for a quote on a repair, Mateo’s breath catches. He finds himself backing toward the door, calculating exits, his gaze darting to the glass display cases, the steel tweezers on his desk, the heavy brass lamp. He knows they are tools, not threats, but his body does not wait for that reasoning. When voices rise during a delivery dispute last spring, the shouting cracks through the workshop like a match to dry wood. He drops his work, shoulders hiking to his ears, certain that the room will tilt into chaos. No matter how often the shop manager or a longtime customer assures him they are safe, the words dissolve the moment a chair scrapes against the floor or a door slams. He watches people’s hands, their posture, the set of their jaws, searching for the flicker of violence before it happens. He tells himself he will never trust an environment until he can hear it without bracing. Over the years, Mateo has refused to sit in his armchair after closing, telling himself that stillness feels like dropping his guard. He keeps his mind occupied, turning over every passing thought like a stone, scanning it for any sign that he is unraveling or losing his grip. When fragments of his childhood home begin to surface, he forces his attention elsewhere, clenching his jaw until the image fractures. These quiet habits have cost him. He has come to believe that his inability to stop the shouting years ago proves he is fundamentally weak. The conviction sits heavy on him, and alongside it, the distance between him and his wider cultural circle has widened. He stops attending the neighborhood festivals, declines invitations to family gatherings, and feels he has lost his place in the community that once raised him. He tells himself he has failed his most important role, a weight he carries without knowing how to set down. The world feels perpetually one loud noise away from collapse. Last week, a new apprentice raised his voice while clarifying a pricing error. Mateo left his station without a word, walked out of the shop, and did not return until closing. That flight, combined with a persistent ache behind his ribs and the exhaustion of constant vigilance, finally pushed him through the clinic’s door. He sits on the edge of the chair now, hands folded tightly, hoping someone can help him unlearn the habit of bracing for impact. What frightens him most is that the workshop, his lifelong anchor, has become a place where he can no longer breathe. He wants, more than anything, to sit at his bench without counting his exits, to look at a man across a table without calculating the distance to the door, and to forgive the boy he was for not being a man then.
